**He'd pass, and fairly quickly.** I'm inferring this from his essays, since as far as I know he hasn't commented on this exact business. His views on tests, writing and admissions all point the same way:

1. **It's a business built on gaming a test.** In "The Lesson to Unlearn" (2019), Graham argues that school trains people to hack tests instead of learning, and that founders have to unlearn this. An AI admissions-essay company doesn't just pick up that habit; it sells it. Its value depends on a gap between what the essay is supposed to measure and what it actually measures.

2. **It removes the thinking the essay exists to show.** "Writes and Write-Nots" (2024) says that writing is thinking, and that AI will split people into those who can write and those who can't. A company that pushes 17-year-olds into the second group at the moment they're asked to show how they think is on the wrong side of his argument.

3. **It conflicts with "Be Good."** Graham says startups that help people do better than ones that exploit them, partly for practical reasons: good people want to work for you and users trust you. Here the users are lying to the admissions office, and your quality depends on that lie going undetected.

4. **The market gets weaker as the product improves.** Once AI essays are common, colleges discount essays or switch to interviews, timed writing or verified samples. His test is whether the business grows with the trend or dies because of it. This one becomes less valuable the better AI gets.

**Where he'd push the founders:** He would probably agree they've spotted something real, namely that the admissions essay is a broken, performative test. His advice would be to build what replaces it, not to sell ways around it. Better ways for colleges to judge applicants, or for students to show real work, is a startup he'd fund. An essay mill with an LLM inside is not.

**Probably not.** The plan wouldn't be the problem. What it says about the founder would be.

In Paul Graham's voice:

A year spent on a business plan before writing any code tells me this founder doesn't yet understand how startups work. You learn what to build by building it and putting it in front of users. A plan written before that contact is mostly fiction, and polishing it for a year means a year of fiction. In "The Hardest Lessons for Startups to Learn" I said the first lesson is to release early. Getting feedback from real users is the whole game, and you can't get it from a document.

There's also a judgment problem. Writing a business plan feels like work and looks like work, which makes it a good way to put off the thing that scares you: making something people might reject. Doing the comfortable, legible task instead of the uncomfortable, important one is exactly what I watch for in founders. I'd much rather see a crude prototype built over a weekend that ten people actually use.

YC has never asked for business plans. When we decide, we're mostly judging the founders. Are they relentlessly resourceful? Do they build things? Do they move fast?

So my default is no. The one exception: if in the interview it turns out they're formidable and they've realized the year was wasted, and they've since built something quickly, I'd consider it. People can learn. But the year of planning counts against them, not for them.

Paul Graham would almost certainly tell you to **move into the same city, ideally the same apartment, at least for the early stage.** He wouldn't treat it as a dealbreaker, but he'd see it as a real handicap you're choosing to take on.

**Why he'd say that, based on what he's written and done:**

1. **YC has always pushed co-location.** For most of YC's history, founders had to come to the Bay Area for the batch. The point was to get founders working intensely side by side, not just to make dinners easier. PG's essays describe early startups as a few people in a room grinding together. *How to Start a Startup* even suggests living together if you can.

2. **Co-founder relationships are the top killer.** In *The 18 Mistakes That Kill Startups*, fights between founders are one of the leading causes of death. Different time zones make that worse. Misunderstandings sit unresolved for hours, decisions get stuck waiting for the other person to wake up, and fewer of your working hours overlap.

3. **Speed is the whole game early on.** He says startups win by doing things fast and iterating with users. A 12-hour feedback loop between co-founders is a self-imposed speed limit at exactly the stage when speed matters most.

4. **Ideas come from casual conversation.** He often credits unplanned talk for the best ideas. Scheduled Zoom calls kill that kind of offhand "what if we…" moment.

**How he'd likely soften it:** After COVID, he and YC accepted remote work much more, and YC ran remote batches. His position seems to have settled on a distinction: **employees can be remote, but founders should be together.** So a fully remote company is fine. Remote co-founders are the part he'd push back on.

**Bottom line in his voice, paraphrased rather than quoted:** you can probably make it work, but why add a handicap? Pick one city and move there. If one of you won't move, that may tell you something about how committed they are.

**No.** Paul Graham would tell you not to take it. His reasons:

1. **It hurts your chances of being acquired by anyone else.** If Google owns a big piece of you, Facebook, Microsoft and Apple will be wary of buying you or partnering with you. You'd effectively be picking your acquirer at the seed stage, before you know what the company is worth. That works against something he cares about a lot: keeping your options open.

2. **It sends a bad signal to other investors.** If Google later decides not to lead your next round, VCs will read that as a judgment about you, and Google knows more about you than they do. A big strategic check turns into a reason others won't invest.

3. **A corporation investing isn't the same as an investor betting on you.** Corporate venture arms have their own strategic goals. Their people change jobs, their priorities shift, and they don't need you to become huge the way a seed investor does. Graham's model of a good early investor is someone whose only interest is your growth.

4. **It distracts you from making something people want.** A big strategic deal often comes with expectations to integrate, build on their platform, or match their roadmap. Early on, your job is to find what users want, not what one partner wants.

5. **You don't need it at seed.** Seed rounds are small. You can raise from angels and seed funds without any of these costs. Graham's broader advice is to take the money that comes with the fewest strings and get back to building.

If Google wants to help, he'd suggest taking a commercial partnership or a small check alongside other investors, with no special rights like board seats, rights of first refusal on an acquisition, or exclusivity. Then revisit at a later round, when you have more leverage and know what you're worth.

This is my reading of his essays and YC's long-standing advice on strategic investors, not a quote of something he said about this exact situation.

**He'd be skeptical. He'd see it as a weak position, and probably as a warning sign about the founders.**

His clearest writing on this is the 2006 essay *"Are Software Patents Evil?"* Its main points:

- **Patents don't protect startups much.** A startup can't afford to enforce a patent against a big company. Even if it could, the lawsuit would take years, and that's time the startup doesn't have. He wrote that the way to protect yourself is to stay ahead technically, not to hold patents. His line was roughly: "the best defense is to be faster."
- **Google is his example.** Google didn't win search because of PageRank's patent. It won by being better and moving faster than competitors who could have copied it.
- **Investors mostly don't care.** He said patents matter a little to acquirers and serve as defensive chips. They don't decide whether YC funds you. What counts is founders who are fast and determined, and users who love the product.
- **It tells him what the founders are thinking.** If a team's answer to "what's your advantage?" is "our patent," he'd take it to mean they think in terms of a moat, not in terms of making something people want and growing fast. To him, an advantage is something you keep earning by staying ahead, not something you file.

**The one caveat:** he admits patents really do matter in fields like biotech and pharma, where one molecule can be the whole business and copying it is easy once it's public. So if this startup is in drug development, his answer would soften. For a software or consumer startup, his verdict would be: the patent is fine to have, but it's not your advantage, so go find a real one.

He'd tell them not to do it. Wanting fame points them at the wrong work, and the bad startup it produces won't make them famous anyway.

This is my paraphrase of how he'd put it, drawn from his essays rather than quoted:

**1. The idea will be bad.** In "How to Get Startup Ideas" he says the best ideas come from noticing a problem you have yourself, not from deciding to start a startup and then looking for an idea. Someone who mainly wants fame is starting a startup for its own sake. That's how you end up with what he calls "made-up" or "sitcom" ideas: plausible-sounding businesses nobody actually wants.

**2. You'll do the work that looks good, not the work that matters.** He keeps warning founders against looking busy instead of making progress. That means press, fundraising announcements, conferences and a big title, when the real job is talking to users and making something people want. Someone after fame will be drawn to the visible parts of a startup, and those are the parts that don't matter early on.

**3. Prestige is a bad guide.** In "How to Do What You Love" he says prestige warps your judgment about what to work on, and calls it "fossilized inspiration." In "How to Do Great Work" he argues the right motive is curiosity about the thing itself. Fame is a result of doing great work. It isn't something you can aim at directly.

**4. You'll quit when it gets hard.** Startups are long and mostly obscure and painful. Fame doesn't arrive in year two, when you're at default-dead and nobody has heard of you. What carries founders through that stretch is caring about the problem and the users. Without that, they give up.

**5. The founders who became famous didn't aim for it.** Jobs, Gates and the Collisons were obsessed with the thing they were building. They got famous because what they built mattered.

**His advice would be:** forget the fame for now. Find a problem you can't stop thinking about, ideally one you have yourself, and build something a small number of people badly want. If it works, they'll get more attention than they wanted. If they can't find a problem they care about more than being known, they shouldn't start a startup yet.

He wouldn't treat ambition as a sin. He likes ambitious founders, and in YC interviews he looks for determination. He'd just say fame is a terrible thing to steer by.

**He'd most likely be skeptical.** He wouldn't object to the technology. He'd object that "Web3 social network" describes how the product is built, not a problem anyone has.

How he'd probably reason, based on his essays:

1. **It sounds like a "sitcom idea."** In *How to Get Startup Ideas* (2012) he warns about ideas that sound plausible, the kind a sitcom writer would give a fictional startup, but that nobody actually wants. A decentralized social network fits that pattern almost exactly. He'd ask: who wants this so badly they'd use a crude version 1 today?

2. **Users don't care what it's built on.** His core test is "make something people want." People join social networks because their friends or the interesting people are already there. Owning your data or your keys has repeatedly failed to pull mainstream users away from incumbents. In 2026, with Farcaster, Lens and Bluesky all having tried, it's clear decentralization alone doesn't get people to switch.

3. **He'd want an organic origin.** He prefers ideas that come from the founder's own need, or that start out looking like a toy. If you're building it because you and a specific group of people actually need it (creators who keep getting deplatformed, a community whose economics really do depend on onchain ownership), he'd become interested. If you're building it because Web3 seemed like the hot category, he'd see that as a red flag.

4. **He'd look past the category at the founders.** His essays suggest a cold-start problem wouldn't stop him if the founders were unusually determined and had a narrow beachhead, meaning one small group that would love the product. "A Web3 Twitter for everyone" fails that test. "The place where X specific people already gather, and crypto is why it works for them" might pass.

**His likely verdict:** Don't start from "Web3 social network." Find a small group with a real, urgent problem. If decentralization turns out to be the reason your solution works for them, that's fine, but it can't be the pitch.

This is an inference from his published essays, not something he has actually said about your idea. I don't have any statement from him on Web3 social networks specifically, so I haven't quoted him on it.

# No. Paul Graham would tell them not to do it.

His reasoning, drawn from his essays:

1. **"Spend little."** This is one of the points in *Startups in 13 Sentences*. Seed money exists to buy runway, meaning time to find product-market fit. A single Super Bowl spot plus production can use up a whole seed round in 30 seconds. In *Default Alive or Default Dead?* he argues that a startup's first job is to avoid dying, and nothing gets you to "default dead" faster than this.

2. **You don't have anything to amplify yet.** An ad scales demand that already exists. At the seed stage you're still learning whether people want the product. His advice in *Do Things That Don't Scale* is the opposite of a mass-market ad: recruit users one at a time by hand and make a small group love you. As he puts it, it's better to have 100 users who love you than a million who kind of like you.

3. **Growth should come from the product.** In *Startup = Growth* he says you should measure real weekly growth and let word of mouth do the work. If the product needs a Super Bowl ad to get noticed, that usually means it isn't good enough yet. Paid attention also gives you a burst of signups that hides that problem.

4. **He has seen this go wrong before.** In 2000, at the peak of the dotcom bubble, a group of startups bought Super Bowl ads (Pets.com is the famous example), and many of them were dead within a year or two. He uses that era as the standard example of startups confusing spending with progress.

**His answer would be roughly:** "Don't. Use the money to stay alive longer and to talk to users. If you build something people want, you won't need the ad, and if you haven't, the ad won't save you."
